Question 76. A conditional geometric family-size law

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original countable mixture bridge

Let P(N=n)=(1−a)an for n≥0, where 0<a<1. Given N, each object's independent attribute occurs with probability b, where 0<b<1. Condition on no object having the attribute. Derive the conditional law of N and P(N≥1) under that condition.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The no-attribute likelihood at size n is (1−b)n, including one at n=0. Joint masses are (1−a)[a(1−b)]n. Their sum is (1−a)/(1−a(1−b)). Question 82. A normalized PMF can have no finite first moment

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original advanced boundary problem

For P(X=k)=1/[k(k+1)], k≥1, verify normalization and determine whether ∑k≥1kp(k) is finite. Explain why this does not invalidate the law.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Normalization telescopes to one as in Question 4. But kp(k)=1/(k+1), whose sum diverges by comparison with the harmonic series. Since all terms are nonnegative, the extended first moment is +∞. A proper countable PMF only requires its mass sum to converge to one; it does not require its value-weighted sum to be finite. Question 83. A complete model audit with a misleading average

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Original integrative conceptual multiple-choice problem

Ten binary devices each work with marginal probability .8. Which conclusion follows without any further dependence assumption? A: Their working count is Bin(10,.8). B: The chance all ten work is .810. C: Each device's individual indicator is Bernoulli .8. D: Their count must attain every integer from zero through ten with positive probability. Construct a counterexample to every false conclusion.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Only C follows: each binary indicator has success mass .8 and failure mass .2. For a single counterexample to A, B, D, let one Bernoulli .8 event decide whether all ten work together. The count then has masses .2 at zero and .8 at ten, and every intermediate count is impossible. All-work probability is .8, not .810. Each individual marginal remains correct. Mutual independence would justify A and B, and with 0<p<1 also give full count support, but it is absent from the contract. A marginal probability cannot supply an unstated joint experiment.

24. Examination rules, edge cases, and final notes

Read these rules after the full derivations. Each rule connects a question trigger to its conditions, computation, and likely error. They are complete statements, not unexplained formulas or generic study advice.

Rule 1

A named random variable is a fixed map. When a question gives elementary outcomes, compute the value on each outcome before assigning a law. In a two-die experiment, the pair and its sum are different objects. Losing the pair can lose dependence information needed for a later question.

Rule 2

Convert values back into events. To evaluate P(X=x), identify every outcome in the fiber {ω:X(ω)=x}. If four outcomes with weights (1,2,3,4)/10 map to (−1,2,−1,5), the mass at −1 is 4/10, not two of four.

Rule 3

Uniform elementary outcomes do not make all measurements uniform. A maximum of two fair four-sided dice has masses (1,3,5,7)/16. Its fiber sizes differ. Use the fiber count divided by the elementary sample-space size only after verifying equal elementary probabilities.

Rule 4

Discrete does not mean integer-valued. A point mass at π is discrete. Integer formulas using F(k)−F(k−1) require integer support; the general jump formula F(x)−F(x−) works at arbitrary real atoms.

Rule 5

A countable law can have accumulating atoms. The values 1/k with masses 2−k approach zero, but no mass remains at zero. Do not infer a continuous component from an accumulation point; check where probability is concentrated.

Rule 6

Distinguish an atom set from its closure. In that 1/k example, zero is in the closure but P(X=0)=0. If an examination uses the word support, identify its convention before declaring that every listed support point has positive mass.

Rule 7

Check every sign separately from normalization. A table (θ,1−3θ,2θ) sums to one identically but is valid only for 0≤θ≤1/3. A solved sum equation does not certify nonnegative probabilities.

Rule 8

Strictly positive support changes endpoint parameter cases. Three positive masses in the preceding table require 0<θ<1/3. At either endpoint the law remains valid, but the effective atom set shrinks. Match strict versus nonstrict parameter wording.

Rule 9

A normalizer cannot repair negative weights. Dividing weights (1,2,−1,2) by their total four leaves a negative mass. Nonnegativity is necessary before interpreting normalization as a probability construction.

Rule 10

Finite sums require the full declared support. For weights k+1 on k=0,…,4, the total is 15. Dropping zero's weight because zero has value zero confuses the mass sum with a value-weighted moment sum.

Rule 11

Infinite normalization needs a limit. For 1/[k(k+1)], partial mass through m is 1−1/(m+1). Its remaining tail is positive, but tends to zero. A finite plot need not contain all probability when it is explicitly labelled a prefix.

Rule 12

Nonnegative sums may be regrouped by fibers. The identity pg(X)(y)=∑g(x)=ypX(x) relies on disjoint atom events and nonnegative probability terms. It does not need continuity or derivatives.

Rule 13

PMF heights are already probabilities. A discrete stem at x has height P(X=x). Do not multiply it by a bin width as if it were a density histogram. Unequal spacing between atoms does not change their masses.

Rule 14

A CDF is defined off support too. With atoms at −2,1,4, F(2.5)=F(1). Interpolating between CDF levels invents probability where the discrete law has none.

Rule 15

A jump's value includes its atom. Since F(t)=P(X≤t), the right-continuous value at a jump is the upper level. A function zero for t≤0 and one for t>0 is not the CDF of a mass at zero.

Rule 16

Use the left limit for strict lower events. F(t−)=P(X<t). For a law with positive mass at t, this differs from F(t). Replacing a strict event by a nonstrict one changes the answer by exactly that atom's mass.

Rule 17

Recover an atom by a jump difference. P(X=t)=F(t)−F(t−). If P(X<2)=1/3 and P(X>2)=1/4, the mass at two is 5/12. The two tails and the atom partition the whole experiment.

Rule 18

The integer difference has a precise condition. For integer-valued X, p(k)=F(k)−F(k−1). On support {0,1/2,1}, using a unit backward step at one would also include the mass at one-half.

Rule 19

An open-lower, closed-upper interval uses ordinary CDF subtraction. For a<X≤b, subtract F(a) from F(b). This removes all outcomes at or below a, including its atom.

Rule 20

A closed lower endpoint needs a left limit. For a≤X≤b, use F(b)−F(a−). With masses (.2,.5,.3) at (−2,1,4), the event 1≤X≤4 has mass .8, not .3.

Rule 21

A strict upper endpoint also needs a left limit. The event a<X<b has probability F(b−)−F(a). A diagram's closed dot at b belongs to the CDF value but must be excluded from this event.

Rule 22

Both half-open directions have different formulas. The event a≤X<b has mass F(b−)−F(a−). Check the lower and upper atoms separately rather than relying on a memorized single interval formula.

Rule 23

For integer support, ceiling and floor encode real bounds. The event .2≤X≤3.9 includes integers one, two, three. Use F(3)−F(0); nearest-integer rounding can wrongly admit zero or four.

Rule 24

Empty feasible intervals have zero mass. If no integer satisfies the supplied bounds, do not accept a negative CDF subtraction from reversed limits. Establish the ordered feasible atom set first.

Rule 25

At least is not strictly greater. For integer r, P(X≥r)=1−F(r−1) while P(X>r)=1−F(r). Their difference is p(r), so a positive atom makes an off-by-one tail error visible.

Rule 26

Every real-variable CDF must reach one in the limit. A curve that remains .8 forever is incomplete or invalid. A disclosed .2 tail at later finite atoms can repair a prefix; putting that mass at infinity changes the type of variable.

Rule 27

Monotonicity cannot replace right continuity. A proposed function can be bounded, nondecreasing, and have limits zero and one yet fail at a jump value. Test the value against the limit from the right at every piecewise boundary.

Rule 28

A continuous increasing segment excludes a purely finite-atom law. A truly linear CDF rise across an interval is not a finite sequence of atom jumps. A smoothed drawing of a discrete CDF must not be interpreted as its exact mathematical graph.

Rule 29

CDF differences determine interval mass, not allocation within it. If F(1)=.2,F(4)=.8, then .6 is allocated among integers two, three, four. Any one of those masses can range from zero through .6 unless extra constraints are given.

Rule 30

Lower quantiles select the first cumulative level reaching the target. For cumulative levels .2,.7,1, a target .7 selects the second atom. A jump can overshoot the target, so F(Q(u))=u need not hold.

Rule 31

An inverse sampler must choose an endpoint contract. Half-open intervals on [0,1) use the first cumulative value strictly exceeding U. At U=.2, the second interval begins. The lower-quantile convention differs on exact boundaries but agrees in law for an ideal continuous uniform input.

Rule 32

Reject uniform input outside the sampler's domain. With a [0,1) contract, input one is invalid. Silently selecting the final atom hides an implementation error; finite digital boundary tests deserve explicit handling.

Rule 33

Simulation frequencies are estimates under their sampling model. A short run need not match a theoretical PMF exactly. Proving a sampler's distribution requires its interval-length or event construction, not a histogram that happens to resemble the expected bars.

Rule 34

A nonlinear measurement adds colliding preimages. For Y=X2, the mass at positive y is the sum over both supported square roots. At zero, there is only one preimage; do not double-count it.

Rule 35

Solve a transform equation within the given support. Algebraic roots outside the source atom set contribute zero. The quadratic X(X−1) can map pairs of integer inputs to the same value; evaluate all valid roots before claiming uniformity.

Rule 36

A negative affine scale reverses both order and inequalities. For Y=aX+b with a<0, FY(t)=1−FX(((t−b)/a)−). The left limit retains boundary mass that belongs to Y≤t.

Rule 37

A zero affine scale is a separate deterministic law. When a=0, all mass lies at b. Inverting by dividing by a would be undefined. A degenerate transformation cannot be treated using the nonzero-scale formulas.

Rule 38

Equal PMFs do not determine an equality event. Fair bits B and 1−B have the same law but never agree. Two independent fair bits agree with probability 1/2. The joint construction distinguishes them.

Rule 39

A single coincident event probability does not establish equal laws. For a uniform three-value X, independent X+Y and the copy sum 2X both have mass 1/3 at four, but only the independent sum can be three. Compare the whole law or a separating event.

Rule 40

Pairwise independence is weaker than mutual independence. The triple (A,B,A⊕B) of fair bits has independent pairs but count support only zero and two. A three-trial binomial requires the full joint factorization.

Rule 41

A Bernoulli indicator can represent a complicated event. If A is a threshold or a multistage success, 1A is still Bernoulli with parameter P(A). The distribution concerns its binary output, not the complexity of the experiment.

Rule 42

Repeating one indicator does not create two trials. For I+I, only zero and two are possible. A nondegenerate Bin(2,p) also has mass at one. Identify whether the problem repeats a variable or independently generates a copy.

Rule 43

Discrete uniform denominators count endpoints. Uniform integers a through b have b−a+1 atoms. For −4 through 8, the denominator is 13. Congruence or parity conditions select a subset of those actual integers.

Rule 44

Modulo maps need equal fiber counts to preserve uniformity. Uniform 0,…,10 modulo 4 gives masses (3,3,3,2)/11. Extending to 11 balances the fibers. The output label count alone cannot supply equal probabilities.

Rule 45

Binomial recognition needs four experiment properties. There must be a fixed n, mutually independent binary trials, a common success probability p, and a success count. Without these, derive the actual law rather than using the family name.

Rule 46

An exact binomial count includes failures. Exactly k successes has factor pk(1−p)n−k. Omitting the failure factor counts selected success witnesses, whose events overlap when additional successes occur.

Rule 47

At least tails sum disjoint exact counts. P(X≥r)=∑k=rnp(k). When r is small, the complement through r−1 can be shorter. For a two-server threshold, network failure includes both zero and one working server.

Rule 48

Binomial endpoint parameters shrink support. At p=0, the count is zero surely; at p=1, it is n surely. Avoid uncontrolled 00 evaluations in code, and exclude zero-mass ratios from adjacent-probability manipulations.

Rule 49

An empty block has zero successes. The n=0 binomial law has one atom at zero. Every normalization and parity identity must agree with that interpretation; an empty experiment is not an undefined count.

Rule 50

Adjacent binomial ratios expose hidden parameters. For 0<p<1, p(k+1)/p(k)=((n−k)/(k+1))(p/(1−p)). Setting such a ratio to a supplied value can eliminate factorials and powers before solving for p.

Rule 51

Binomial mode ties occur at an exact integer boundary. If (n+1)p=m is integer, the modes are m−1,m. For n=9,p=.4, these are three and four. Rounding np is not the exact mode rule.

Rule 52

Binomial even-count probabilities need not be one-half. The formula is [1+(1−2p)n]/2 for n≥1. It follows by adding the normalized and signed expansions. At p=1/4,n=4, the answer is 17/32.

Rule 53

Two-stage eligibility can be collapsed per object. Independent qualification a followed by conditional success b gives per-object success ab. Across independent objects, the final count is Bin(n,ab). Retain the qualification event when defining success.

Rule 54

Conditioning on the eligible count provides an independent derivation. Sum P(K=k)P(Y=r∣K=k) over feasible k. Replacing K by its mean changes the experiment and generally loses the correct count law.

Rule 55

Independent unequal probabilities produce a Poisson-binomial count. Multiply ∏j((1−pj)+pjz) or propagate dynamic probability rows. Averaging the pj can preserve a mean while changing individual count masses.

Rule 56

A common random probability creates a mixture. Choosing one coin for an entire block makes later tosses dependent after the regime is hidden. Average conditional laws; do not substitute the average p into one binomial without proving unconditional independence.

Rule 57

The timing of a latent choice is decisive. Reselecting an independent coin before each toss can make fair independent outcomes; selecting once can give masses (5,6,5)/16 on a two-toss count. State which random choice is shared.

Rule 58

A stopped series can use an imagined fixed horizon correctly. Pre-generate the unplayed outcomes and compare the final majority event. That construction can prove a winning probability, but it does not make the actual stopping-time distribution binomial.

Rule 59

Hypergeometric parameters are finite integers. Require 0≤K≤N and 0≤n≤N. A numerical root for K outside this integer range cannot describe the population, even if it solves an algebraic probability equation.

Rule 60

Hypergeometric lower support is often positive. The bound k≥max(0,n−(N−K)) forces successes when failures cannot fill the sample. Drawing seven of eight objects with three successes forces at least two marked objects.

Rule 61

The hypergeometric numerator chooses both categories. Use (Kk)(N−Kn−k) over (Nn). Omitting the failure choice or using n! as the denominator counts a different collection of elementary objects.

Rule 62

Without-replacement sequential probabilities change with the state. After j draws and k successes, the next success chance is (K−k)/(N−j). A constant K/N at every draw silently inserts replacement.

Rule 63

Ordered and unordered derivations can agree without sharing denominators. For four successes among ten and three draws, the three two-success patterns each have mass 1/10. Their sum 3/10 matches the subset formula 36/120.

Rule 64

Observed urn draws update both composition and remaining target. Given a first success, the remaining successful-object count decreases by one, and a target total of two requires one more success. Reusing the original parameters ignores the observation.

Rule 65

Geometric trial count starts at one; failure count starts at zero. T=G+1 implies P(T=t)=pqt−1 and P(G=g)=pqg. A family name without its convention is incomplete information.

Rule 66

Geometric survival counts prior failures exactly. For integer m≥0, P(T>m)=qm and P(T≥m+1)=qm. At least four total attempts needs three initial failures, not four.

Rule 67

A real geometric threshold uses a floor. For x≥1, FT(x)=1−q⌊x⌋. A threshold 3.9 admits times through three. A continuous interpolation changes the law.

Rule 68

Geometric properness requires positive success probability. At p=0, finite stopping masses sum to zero and nontermination is certain. At p=1, waiting is immediate; conditioning on later survival is impossible.

Rule 69

Memorylessness is conditional on a nonzero survival event. Cancel qs only when P(T>s)>0. The remaining iid trials then give P(T>s+t∣T>s)=qt. Do not retain a factor charging failures already observed.

Rule 70

Varying independent hazards do not give geometric memorylessness. Survival is ∏j=1m(1−pj). Independence supports the product, but a common p is needed for a fixed geometric power and elapsed-time invariance.

Rule 71

Capping accumulates the whole tail into the last atom. For W=min(T,c), P(W=c)=qc−1. This includes success at c and all later stopping times. Using pqc−1 would omit censored nontermination-by-cap histories.

Rule 72

Conditioning on success by a cap instead renormalizes. Divide pqt−1 by 1−qc for t=1,…,c. This differs from capping; for fair trials with c=4, the final probabilities are 1/15 and 1/8 respectively.

Rule 73

A distinct no-success output preserves a separate mass. With c attempts, the no-success code has mass qc, while success on the final attempt has mass pqc−1. State whether the output merges or distinguishes them.

Rule 74

Negative-binomial stopping forces the final success. For total trials through r successes, use (t−1r−1)prqt−r. Choosing r positions from all t would allow a failed last trial after an earlier completion.

Rule 75

Failures and total trials differ by r, not one. Gr=Tr−r. Substitute t=g+r before selecting the coefficient (g+r−1r−1). The one-success geometric offset is only the r=1 special case.

Rule 76

A fixed-time binomial event answers a negative-binomial CDF. Tr≤m if and only if at least r of the first m trials succeed. This gives the correct tail while preserving the different support and meaning of Tr.

Rule 77

Poisson parameters belong to a specified observation window. Under a supplied homogeneous rate model, convert units and use λ=rt. A stated average count alone does not prove a Poisson law. Normalization comes from the exponential series.

Rule 78

Poisson adjacent ratios determine modes and parameters. p(k+1)/p(k)=λ/(k+1). At positive integer λ=m, two modes m−1,m tie. The zero-parameter law is a separate point mass with one mode.

Rule 79

A Poisson approximation is not a finite identity. (1−1/n)n approaches e−1 but differs at every finite n>1. A displayed finite prefix also has a genuine omitted tail; renormalizing it produces a conditional law rather than the original Poisson.

Rule 80

Validate the whole experiment before transferring a formula. Joint independence enables convolution products and maximum-CDF products; support permits legal indices; nonzero conditioning mass permits division; finite-moment assumptions govern expectation later. Use an explicit counterexample such as all devices succeeding together to diagnose which missing condition changes the answer.

25. Editable distribution laboratory

Choose a model and edit its stated inputs. Each computation begins paused and exposes its exact stored states, operation, cause, probability checks and state changes. Finite diagrams illustrate a specified calculation; their checkpoints are not proofs about every possible input. Infinite laws display a prefix with a separately labelled omitted tail. The written arguments supply general proofs.

CDF, interval, quantile and square modes use 1–8 atom values and equally long nonnegative mass lists summing to one. Duplicate atom values merge; unnormalized weights are rejected. Interval mode uses the lower and upper bounds. Quantile mode uses a probability level in (0,1]. Binomial uses integer n from 0 to 12 and p in [0,1]. Geometric uses p in (0,1]. Poisson uses lambda in [0,10]. Hypergeometric uses integer population N from 1 to 20, marked count K from 0 to N, and sample size from 0 to N. Named-family modes ignore the value and mass lists after basic input syntax checks. Every infinite-law prefix retains an explicit omitted tail. Invalid input preserves the previous model. Display arithmetic is rounded; the underlying state retains double precision and the audits separately check exact rational fixtures.
